common_name: Moon and Stars Watermelon (Star-Speckled Heirloom Watermelon)

planting.note: Direct sow after all frost danger has passed and soil has warmed to at least 70°F, in deeply worked, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; give vines 8-10 feet of room to sprawl.

directions: Sow in fertile, well-drained, deeply worked soil in full sun once soil has warmed; keep evenly watered through fruit set and ease off watering as melons near ripeness. Moon and Stars is a striking American heirloom watermelon, first documented in the late 1800s and rescued from near-extinction in the 1980s after seed saver Merle Van Doren shared surviving seed with Kent Whealy of Seed Savers Exchange, reviving a variety that had all but vanished from commerce. Its dark green rind is scattered with one large yellow 'moon' spot and many smaller yellow 'star' speckles, a genetically distinctive and instantly recognizable pattern; the leaves also show smaller yellow speckling, making the plant ornamental even before fruiting. Flesh is sweet, deep red, and classic in flavor, and large fruits commonly reach 20-40 pounds. Because it is an open-pollinated heirloom, seed saves true when isolated from other watermelon varieties, making it a favorite for gardeners who want to preserve genetic and horticultural history alongside a tasty harvest.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Moon and Stars variety history

common_name: Dixie Queen Watermelon (Round Striped Southern Heirloom)

planting.note: Direct sow after all frost danger has passed and soil has warmed to at least 70°F, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; give vines 6-8 feet of room to sprawl.

directions: Sow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once soil has warmed; keep evenly watered through fruit set and ease off watering as melons near ripeness to concentrate sugars. Dixie Queen is a classic Southern heirloom watermelon dating to the early 20th century, producing round-to-oval fruit with light and dark green striping and sweet, bright red flesh with good old-fashioned watermelon flavor. It was once a popular commercial variety before being largely displaced by modern hybrids bred for tougher rinds and shipping durability, but it remains a favorite among heirloom growers for its reliable production and classic taste in the home garden. Vines are vigorous and productive over a moderate-length season, and fruits typically run in the 15-25 pound range, a manageable size for home use. As an open-pollinated heirloom, seed saves true when isolated from other watermelon varieties.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Dixie Queen variety notes
